source.title: Expand More, Shrink Less: Shaping Effective-Rank Dynamics for Dense Scaling in Recommendation
source.authors: Guo-Ming Li; Shang-Yu Zhang; Jun-Wei Pan; Wentao Ning; Jin Chen; Gengsheng Xue; Chao Zhou; Shu-Dong Huang; Hai-Jie Gu; Meng-Lin Yang

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports parameter-scaling results for recommendation models, extending scaling analysis to a different model domain and downstream task; it does not study language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper's scaling experiments measure recommendation AUC and LogLoss as dense parameters are scaled. They bear on V6 in recommendation settings. They do not measure language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy, test small-run extrapolation, find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or establish that architecture details have little effect. Exact curve values are presented only in figures; cited language-model scaling findings are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: This is a recommender-architecture paper. Its 'scaling-law experiments' sweep dense parameters only 1x–9x (under one order of magnitude) to show RankElastor scales better than RankMixer. It reports no power-law form, exponents or extrapolation, and its CTR AUC/LogLoss values appear only in figures. That makes it a comparison of its own method's performance, not a test of language-model scaling laws. It is also not the downstream-from-pretraining predictability that V6 names, so the reader's V6 link is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that RankElastor mitigates embedding collapse (higher effective rank), improves CTR performance over RankMixer and other baselines, and shows better dense-parameter scaling than RankMixer. They also find joint depth+width scaling beats single-dimension scaling, which they say aligns with Kaplan et al.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales depth and FFN width in recommendation architectures and evaluates CTR metrics, rather than measuring language-model pretraining loss across parameter, token, or compute budgets.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports width-wise, depth-wise, and joint depth-and-width scaling separately; joint scaling is described as yielding larger gains than scaling one dimension alone.

fits_no_version.finding: For two CTR recommender architectures on Criteo and Avazu, test AUC rises and LogLoss falls as dense parameters grow 1x–9x. Joint depth+width scaling gains more than scaling one dimension, and RankElastor gains more than RankMixer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over a narrow (<10x) range, recommendation-model held-out loss improves monotonically with dense parameters, and the slope depends on architecture.

record.problems: Scaling curve values are shown only in figures and are not tabulated in the text. The study reports results averaged over 10 runs for its standard experiments, but gives no uncertainty estimates for the scaling curves. Its scaling evidence concerns recommendation metrics, not language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No separately described scaling sweep was left out. Individual plotted markers are retained as figure-only sweep results rather than transcribed as separate numeric values because the text does not state their values.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss, no multi-order-of-magnitude sweep.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: shape is not varied at fixed parameter count; depth and width sweeps change parameter count.
Power-law form in another domain: the fitted curve form is unstated and the range is <1 order of magnitude.
All: no LM downstream tasks and no prediction from pretraining loss.
All: no comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan et al. is cited only for the depth+width remark. The reader's V6 'supports' label is removed: CTR metrics in a method comparison don't bear on LM downstream predictability. The study gives no values, functional form or exponents for the fitted dashed curves.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its dependence on compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests recommendation performance under parameter scaling, not language-model downstream task performance or predictability from pretraining loss.
Whether fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup and fitting choices, or whether curves bend away from a single power law.
